courses.title: Operating Theatre Essentials
courses.subtitle: Find your way round theatre, work safely in the team and keep the field sterile.
courses.description: Find your way round theatre, work safely in the team and keep the field sterile.
outcomes: Describe the layout of an operating theatre and the role of each team member
Run the three phases of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
Perform a surgical hand scrub, closed gowning and gloving
Set up and maintain a sterile field and recognise when it is breached
Agree an opening count and complete a closing count

modules.title: The theatre and the team
modules.summary: Who does what, where, and why it matters to the patient.

lessons.title: Theatre layout and zones
lessons.summary: An operating suite is divided into unrestricted, semi-restricted and restricted zones.
lessons.content: An operating suite is divided into unrestricted, semi-restricted and restricted zones. Theatre attire is worn in the semi-restricted zone; masks are added in the restricted zone, where the sterile field is open. Air flows from the cleanest area (over the table) outwards, so doors stay closed and traffic is kept to a minimum. Learn where the scrub sink, anaesthetic room, sterile store and dirty utility sit in your own hospital: on day one you should be able to reach each without crossing the sterile field.

lessons.title: Roles in the theatre team
lessons.summary: The operating surgeon and assistant are scrubbed; the scrub practitioner owns the instruments, the sterile field and the counts; the circulating practitioner is unscrubbed and fetches, opens and records; the anaesthetist and anaesthetic practitioner own the airway, drugs and monitoring.
lessons.content: The operating surgeon and assistant are scrubbed; the scrub practitioner owns the instruments, the sterile field and the counts; the circulating practitioner is unscrubbed and fetches, opens and records; the anaesthetist and anaesthetic practitioner own the airway, drugs and monitoring. Anyone, including a student, may and must speak up about a sterility breach or a safety concern.

lessons.title: Meet the theatre equipment
lessons.summary: Walk round the core equipment of a theatre; open, raise and move each working part.

lessons.title: Set up the theatre equipment
lessons.summary: Plug in the generator, monitor, suction and tower; put the monitoring and the diathermy plate on the patient.

lessons.title: Check: theatre and team
lessons.summary: 2 questions with feedback.

questions.prompt: Who is primarily responsible for the instrument and swab count?

options.text: The scrub practitioner, with the circulator
options.feedback: The scrub and circulating practitioners count aloud together and record it; the surgeon is told and confirms.
Not quite: The scrub and circulating practitioners count aloud together and record it; the surgeon is told and confirms.
The surgeon confirms, but the count is run by the scrub and circulating practitioners.

questions.prompt: A student notices a gloved assistant touch the unsterile light handle. What should they do?

options.feedback: Any breach is called out at once so the glove can be changed before it touches the field.

options.text: Say nothing; students should not interrupt
options.feedback: Everyone in theatre has a duty to speak up about a breach.

options.text: Mention it at the end of the case
options.feedback: By then the contamination may have reached the wound.

modules.title: Safety checklist
modules.summary: Sign in, time out, sign out.

lessons.title: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
lessons.summary: Sign In happens before induction: identity, site, procedure and consent are confirmed, the site is marked, the anaesthesia machine and pulse oximeter are checked, and allergies, airway risk and expected blood loss are reviewed.
lessons.content: Sign In happens before induction: identity, site, procedure and consent are confirmed, the site is marked, the anaesthesia machine and pulse oximeter are checked, and allergies, airway risk and expected blood loss are reviewed. Time Out happens before skin incision: the whole team introduces itself, confirms patient, site and procedure, antibiotic prophylaxis within the last 60 minutes, anticipated critical events and imaging. Sign Out happens before the patient leaves: the procedure recorded, counts correct, specimens labelled, equipment problems and recovery concerns handed over.

lessons.title: Check: the checklist
lessons.summary: 2 questions with feedback.

questions.prompt: When is the Time Out performed?

options.feedback: Time Out is the last pause before the knife touches skin.
That is the Sign In.
That is the Sign Out.

questions.prompt: Antibiotic prophylaxis for most clean-contaminated cases is ideally given…

options.feedback: Tissue levels must be adequate at the moment of incision; most agents are given within 60 minutes before it.
Too late to be in the tissues when contamination happens.
Not quite: Tissue levels must be adequate at the moment of incision; most agents are given within 60 minutes before it.

lessons.title: Surgical hand antisepsis
lessons.summary: Remove jewellery, keep nails short and unvarnished.
lessons.content: Remove jewellery, keep nails short and unvarnished. A first scrub of the day starts with a wash to remove debris, cleaning under the nails. With an antiseptic scrub (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine) scrub hands then forearms to 2 cm above the elbow for the time in your local policy (typically 2–5 minutes), keeping hands above elbows so water runs off the elbows. Alcohol-based surgical hand rubs are an accepted alternative on clean, dry hands. Dry with a sterile towel from fingertips to elbow, one side of the towel per arm.

lessons.title: Scrub at the sink
lessons.summary: Scrub with the demonstration hands; each step is recognised from your hand movement.

lessons.title: Closed gowning and gloving
lessons.summary: Pick up the gown by the inside of the neckband, let it unfold away from you, slide your arms in without letting your hands leave the cuffs.
lessons.content: Pick up the gown by the inside of the neckband, let it unfold away from you, slide your arms in without letting your hands leave the cuffs. Glove through the gown sleeve (closed technique), then tie the gown with a sterile turn. Your sterile area is the front of the gown from chest to table level and the sleeves from 5 cm above the elbow to the cuff: hands stay in it, clasped in front.

lessons.title: Check: scrubbing
lessons.summary: 2 questions with feedback.

questions.prompt: Which part of a sterile gown is considered sterile?

options.text: Front from chest to table level, and the sleeves
options.feedback: Front chest-to-table and sleeves to just above the elbow are the sterile zone.

options.text: The whole gown including the back
options.feedback: The back cannot be watched and is not sterile.
Not quite: Front chest-to-table and sleeves to just above the elbow are the sterile zone.

questions.prompt: During the scrub, hands are held…

options.feedback: Water must drain from the clean hands towards the elbows.
Water would run from the unscrubbed arm onto the hands.

options.text: At any height as long as the brush is used
options.feedback: Not quite: Water must drain from the clean hands towards the elbows.

lessons.title: Maintaining the sterile field
lessons.summary: Only sterile items touch sterile items.
lessons.content: Only sterile items touch sterile items. Sterile tables are sterile only at table height; anything that drops below the waist or the table edge is contaminated. Never turn your back on the field, never reach across an unsterile area, and keep two sterile people front-to-front or back-to-back when passing. If in doubt, consider it contaminated and replace it.

lessons.title: Counts
lessons.summary: Swabs, sharps and instruments are counted aloud by two people before the procedure (the opening count), before closing a cavity, before skin closure and at the end.
lessons.content: Swabs, sharps and instruments are counted aloud by two people before the procedure (the opening count), before closing a cavity, before skin closure and at the end. Swabs are counted in their packs of five, separated, with the radio-opaque marker visible. A discrepancy stops closure until the item is found or an X-ray is taken.

lessons.title: Back table check and opening count
lessons.summary: Check the sterile back table, count instruments and swabs, then drape the patient.

lessons.title: Assessment: prepare for surgery
lessons.summary: Scrub, gown, glove, count and drape with no guidance.

courses.title: Surgical Instruments and Handling
courses.subtitle: Know every instrument on the tray, hold it properly and pass it safely.
courses.description: Know every instrument on the tray, hold it properly and pass it safely.

modules.title: Instrument families
modules.summary: Cutting, grasping, clamping, retracting and suction.

lessons.title: The five families
lessons.summary: Cutting: scalpels, scissors (Mayo for tougher tissue and sutures, Metzenbaum for delicate dissection), bone saws and rongeurs.
lessons.content: Cutting: scalpels, scissors (Mayo for tougher tissue and sutures, Metzenbaum for delicate dissection), bone saws and rongeurs. Grasping: toothed forceps for skin and fascia, non-toothed (atraumatic) forceps for bowel and vessels. Clamping: artery forceps (haemostats) with a ratchet, Kocher clamps with teeth, bowel clamps. Retracting: hand-held (Langenbeck, Deaver, rake) and self-retaining (Weitlaner, Balfour). Suction: Yankauer for open fields, Poole for the abdomen, fine suction for small spaces.

lessons.title: The instrument tray
lessons.summary: Pick up each instrument, open its jaws and lock the ratchets; its name and use appear as you hold it.

lessons.summary: 2 questions with feedback.

options.feedback: Bowel and vessels are handled with atraumatic instruments.
Teeth puncture bowel.
Kochers have teeth and crush tissue.

questions.prompt: A self-retaining retractor is chosen when…

options.text: The assistant's hands are needed for other tasks
options.feedback: Self-retaining retractors hold the wound open without an assistant.
Not quite: Self-retaining retractors hold the wound open without an assistant.
Not quite: Self-retaining retractors hold the wound open without an assistant.

lessons.title: Grips
lessons.summary: Scalpel: the 'dinner knife' grip for long skin incisions with a No.
lessons.content: Scalpel: the 'dinner knife' grip for long skin incisions with a No. 10 blade; the pen grip for fine work with a No. 15. Forceps: held like a pen, never in the palm. Scissors and needle holders: tripod grip with thumb and ring finger in the rings and the index finger on the shaft for stability; cut with the tips. Never use the fingers to pick up needles.

lessons.title: Passing instruments and sharps safety
lessons.summary: Instruments are passed handle first into the surgeon's palm, curved instruments with the curve matching the surgeon's hand.
lessons.content: Instruments are passed handle first into the surgeon's palm, curved instruments with the curve matching the surgeon's hand. Sharps are passed in a neutral zone (a kidney dish) rather than hand to hand, scalpels are loaded and unloaded with a needle holder, and every needle is accounted for at the end of the count.

lessons.title: Instrument handling at the skills station
lessons.summary: Pick, grip and pass the open-surgery instruments at the skills-lab station.

questions.prompt: Scalpel blades should be loaded…

options.text: With a needle holder, never with fingers
options.feedback: Using a needle holder keeps fingers away from the edge.
Not quite: Using a needle holder keeps fingers away from the edge.

courses.title: Wound Closure and Suturing
courses.subtitle: Choose the right suture and needle, tie secure knots and close skin neatly.
courses.description: Choose the right suture and needle, tie secure knots and close skin neatly.
outcomes: Choose suture material and needle for a given tissue
Tie a two-handed reef knot and an instrument tie
Place simple interrupted, mattress and subcuticular sutures
Describe the alternatives: staples, adhesive strips and tissue glue

lessons.title: Choosing a suture
lessons.summary: Absorbable sutures (e.g.
lessons.content: Absorbable sutures (e.g. polyglactin, poliglecaprone, PDS) lose strength over weeks and suit deep layers and subcuticular skin. Non-absorbable sutures (nylon, polypropylene) keep strength and suit skin sutures that will be removed and vascular anastomoses. Monofilaments slide and resist infection but need more throws; braided sutures handle well but can harbour bacteria. Sizes run from 0 (thick) to 10-0 (finest): 3-0 or 4-0 for most skin, 5-0/6-0 on the face. Cutting needles go through skin; round-bodied needles through bowel and soft tissue.

lessons.title: Needles, holders and closure devices
lessons.summary: Look at needle shapes and sizes, a ligature needle and a skin stapler.

lessons.title: Check: materials
lessons.summary: 2 questions with feedback.

questions.prompt: Which needle is used for skin?

options.feedback: A cutting edge passes through tough dermis.
Round-bodied needles are for soft tissue and bowel.
Not quite: A cutting edge passes through tough dermis.

questions.prompt: A monofilament suture needs…

options.feedback: Monofilaments are slippery, so knots need extra throws.
Not quite: Monofilaments are slippery, so knots need extra throws.
Not quite: Monofilaments are slippery, so knots need extra throws.

modules.title: Knots and stitches
modules.summary: From the reef knot to subcuticular closure.

lessons.title: Knot tying
lessons.summary: A square (reef) knot is two throws in opposite directions laid flat; a surgeon's knot adds a double first throw so the first tie holds under tension.
lessons.content: A square (reef) knot is two throws in opposite directions laid flat; a surgeon's knot adds a double first throw so the first tie holds under tension. Instrument ties save suture and are quick for skin. Tension each throw by moving the hands in the plane of the knot and beyond it; never saw the suture or lift the tissue.

lessons.title: Stitches
lessons.summary: Simple interrupted: enter at 90°, equal bites either side (about as far from the edge as the skin is thick), evert the edges.
lessons.content: Simple interrupted: enter at 90°, equal bites either side (about as far from the edge as the skin is thick), evert the edges. Vertical mattress: far-far then near-near for eversion in thin or lax skin. Horizontal mattress: spreads tension. Subcuticular: continuous in the dermis for the best cosmetic result. Approximate, don't strangulate: tissue swells after closure.

lessons.title: Suturing practice pad
lessons.summary: Place interrupted and mattress sutures on a skin pad and tie instrument knots.

lessons.title: Assessment: close the wound
lessons.summary: Close a 5 cm wound with interrupted sutures, scored on spacing, eversion and knot security.

courses.title: Asepsis and Infection Prevention
courses.subtitle: Prevent surgical site infection from the ward to the wound.
courses.description: Prevent surgical site infection from the ward to the wound.
outcomes: Explain how surgical site infection develops and is classified
Apply the SSI prevention bundle: skin prep, hair removal, normothermia, glucose, antibiotics
Decontaminate and sterilise instruments and explain the sterile-processing cycle
frameworks: WHO Global Guidelines for SSI Prevention

lessons.title: Wound classes and SSI
lessons.summary: Wounds are classed clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated or dirty, and the risk of infection rises with each.
lessons.content: Wounds are classed clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated or dirty, and the risk of infection rises with each. SSIs are superficial, deep or organ/space and are counted up to 30 days after surgery (90 with an implant). The prevention bundle: no routine hair removal (clippers, not razors, if needed), alcohol-based chlorhexidine skin preparation allowed to dry, prophylactic antibiotics within 60 minutes before incision, normothermia, glucose control and minimal theatre traffic.

lessons.title: Skin preparation and draping
lessons.summary: Prepare from the incision site outwards in widening areas, never back towards the centre, covering enough skin for drains and an extended incision.
lessons.content: Prepare from the incision site outwards in widening areas, never back towards the centre, covering enough skin for drains and an extended incision. Alcohol-based preparations are flammable: let them dry fully before diathermy and drapes. Drapes are placed from the incision outwards and never moved towards it once placed.

lessons.title: Sterile processing
lessons.summary: Open sterilising containers and trays and see how a tray is assembled.

options.text: Clippers, close to the time of surgery
options.feedback: Clipping avoids skin trauma; shaving increases SSI.

Not quite: Clipping avoids skin trauma; shaving increases SSI.

questions.prompt: Why must alcoholic skin prep dry before diathermy?

courses.title: Perioperative Patient Safety
courses.subtitle: Consent, marking, VTE, anticoagulation, fasting and handover.
courses.description: Consent, marking, VTE, anticoagulation, fasting and handover.
outcomes: Take valid informed consent and know when you may not
Prescribe VTE prophylaxis and manage anticoagulants around surgery
Apply fasting guidance and hand over safely using SBAR

lessons.title: Informed consent
lessons.summary: Consent is valid when the patient has capacity, is informed (the nature of the procedure, its purpose, material risks, alternatives including doing nothing) and decides voluntarily.
lessons.content: Consent is valid when the patient has capacity, is informed (the nature of the procedure, its purpose, material risks, alternatives including doing nothing) and decides voluntarily. The person taking consent must be able to perform the procedure or be trained to consent for it. Material risks are those a reasonable person in the patient's position would want to know, or this patient would.

lessons.title: VTE, anticoagulants and fasting
lessons.summary: Assess every patient for venous thromboembolism and bleeding risk; offer mechanical and/or pharmacological prophylaxis by risk.
lessons.content: Assess every patient for venous thromboembolism and bleeding risk; offer mechanical and/or pharmacological prophylaxis by risk. Plan anticoagulant and antiplatelet interruption with the prescriber, weighing thrombotic against bleeding risk. Typical elective fasting: food until 6 hours, clear fluids until 2 hours before anaesthesia (check your local policy).

lessons.summary: 2 questions with feedback.

questions.prompt: Which of these is required for valid consent?

options.feedback: Consent is a process: capacity, information, voluntary choice.
The signature is evidence, not consent itself.

options.text: Agreement of the next of kin
options.feedback: Adults with capacity decide for themselves.

courses.title: Energy Devices in Surgery
courses.subtitle: Use monopolar, bipolar and advanced energy safely.
courses.description: Use monopolar, bipolar and advanced energy safely.
outcomes: Explain how monopolar and bipolar diathermy work
Prevent burns: return electrode, alcohol prep, insulation failure and capacitive coupling
Choose cut, coagulation or advanced bipolar/ultrasonic energy for a task

lessons.title: Monopolar and bipolar
lessons.summary: In monopolar diathermy current flows from the active electrode through the patient to a return pad; in bipolar it flows only between the two tips.
lessons.content: In monopolar diathermy current flows from the active electrode through the patient to a return pad; in bipolar it flows only between the two tips. Cut uses a continuous low-voltage waveform that vaporises cells; coagulation uses an interrupted high-voltage waveform. Burns occur at a poorly applied return pad, through pooled alcohol, by direct coupling to another instrument, through insulation failure or by capacitive coupling in laparoscopy. Bipolar is preferred near nerves, in fingers and penis, and around pacemakers.

lessons.title: The electrosurgical unit
lessons.summary: Explore the generator, its leads and a bipolar instrument.

options.text: Only between the two tips of the instrument
options.feedback: Bipolar does not need a return electrode.

options.text: Through the patient to a return pad
options.feedback: That is monopolar.

courses.subtitle: What the anaesthetist is doing, and what the numbers on the monitor mean.

modules.title: The anaesthetic side of the screen

lessons.title: Monitoring
lessons.summary: Minimum monitoring during anaesthesia: ECG, pulse oximetry, non-invasive blood pressure, capnography and anaesthetic gas analysis, with temperature for longer cases.
lessons.content: Minimum monitoring during anaesthesia: ECG, pulse oximetry, non-invasive blood pressure, capnography and anaesthetic gas analysis, with temperature for longer cases. A falling end-tidal CO2 can mean a disconnection, a pulmonary embolism or low cardiac output; a rising heart rate with falling blood pressure in surgery is bleeding until proven otherwise.

lessons.title: Local anaesthetic doses
lessons.summary: Commonly quoted maximum doses: lidocaine 3 mg/kg plain and 7 mg/kg with adrenaline; bupivacaine 2 mg/kg.
lessons.content: Commonly quoted maximum doses: lidocaine 3 mg/kg plain and 7 mg/kg with adrenaline; bupivacaine 2 mg/kg. A 1 % solution contains 10 mg/ml. Toxicity starts with perioral tingling, tinnitus and agitation, then seizures and cardiovascular collapse; treat with airway support and intravenous lipid emulsion. Always check your local formulary.

lessons.summary: Explore the anaesthetic machine, ventilator, infusion pumps and monitoring.

lessons.title: NOTSS
lessons.summary: The Non-Technical Skills for Surgeons framework has four categories: situation awareness (gather, understand, anticipate), decision making (consider options, select and communicate, review), communication and teamwork (exchange information, establish shared understanding, coordinate), and leadership (set standards, support others, cope with pressure)..
lessons.content: The Non-Technical Skills for Surgeons framework has four categories: situation awareness (gather, understand, anticipate), decision making (consider options, select and communicate, review), communication and teamwork (exchange information, establish shared understanding, coordinate), and leadership (set standards, support others, cope with pressure).

lessons.summary: Use closed-loop communication: the instruction, the read-back, the confirmation.
lessons.content: Use closed-loop communication: the instruction, the read-back, the confirmation. When concerned, escalate with graded assertiveness, for example the PACE steps: Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency. A stop word agreed at the briefing lets anyone halt the procedure.

lessons.title: The laparoscopic stack
lessons.summary: The stack holds the camera control unit, light source, insufflator, recorder and monitor.
lessons.content: The stack holds the camera control unit, light source, insufflator, recorder and monitor. A poor image is usually a dirty or fogged lens, white balance not done, a loose light cable or blood in the field. The insufflator delivers CO2, typically to 12–15 mmHg in adults; higher pressure reduces venous return and splints the diaphragm.

lessons.title: Entry and port placement
lessons.summary: Open (Hasson) entry at the umbilicus is preferred by many guidelines; Veress needle and optical entry are alternatives with their own precautions.
lessons.content: Open (Hasson) entry at the umbilicus is preferred by many guidelines; Veress needle and optical entry are alternatives with their own precautions. Working ports are placed under vision, away from the epigastric vessels, triangulated so the instruments meet the target at about 60° and the camera sits between them. Insert trocars perpendicular to the skin and then angle towards the target, with controlled force.

lessons.title: The fulcrum effect
lessons.summary: A laparoscopic instrument pivots at the abdominal wall: move the hand left and the tip goes right, move it up and the tip goes down.
lessons.content: A laparoscopic instrument pivots at the abdominal wall: move the hand left and the tip goes right, move it up and the tip goes down. The ratio of inside to outside length scales tip movement. Depth comes from cues on a 2D screen: shadows, size and instrument contact. Deliberate practice of standard tasks (peg transfer, precision cutting, ligating loop, intra- and extracorporeal knots) builds these skills measurably.

lessons.title: The critical view of safety
lessons.summary: Before any structure is clipped: the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue, the lower third of the gallbladder is separated from the liver bed, and exactly two structures are seen entering the gallbladder.
lessons.content: Before any structure is clipped: the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue, the lower third of the gallbladder is separated from the liver bed, and exactly two structures are seen entering the gallbladder. If it cannot be achieved, stop and consider a bail-out: subtotal cholecystectomy, cholangiography or calling for help.

modules.title: Scrubbing for a case
modules.summary: Setting up and running the field.

lessons.title: Back table and Mayo stand
lessons.summary: Open the outer wraps away from you, check sterility indicators and tray lists, then lay out instruments in the order they will be used.
lessons.content: Open the outer wraps away from you, check sterility indicators and tray lists, then lay out instruments in the order they will be used. The Mayo stand holds what the surgeon needs next. Keep sharps in one place and account for every item.

lessons.title: Trays, carts and containers
lessons.summary: Open drawers, lids and trays and see how a case is set up.

lessons.title: Back table and count
lessons.summary: Agree the opening count at the back table.

lessons.title: Closing count
lessons.summary: Find the hidden swab and complete the closing count.

courses.title: Infusion Devices and Patient Equipment
courses.subtitle: Infusion pumps, syringe drivers, suction, oxygen and monitoring.
courses.description: Infusion pumps, syringe drivers, suction, oxygen and monitoring.
outcomes: Set up an infusion pump and syringe driver safely
Set up suction and oxygen delivery
Respond to equipment alarms

lessons.title: Infusion devices
lessons.summary: Volumetric pumps deliver fluids from bags; syringe drivers deliver small precise volumes.
lessons.content: Volumetric pumps deliver fluids from bags; syringe drivers deliver small precise volumes. Check the drug, dose, rate and line against the prescription, use drug libraries, and never silence an alarm without finding its cause (occlusion, air in line, end of infusion).

lessons.title: Bedside devices
lessons.summary: Operate the infusion pump door, syringe plunger, nebuliser and more.
